references.text: "In the beginning" (Ἐν ἀρχῇ) is a direct echo of [ref:1 Mos 1:1|Genesis 1:1]: "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth." John places the existence of the Word before creation itself, thereby linking the Logos to the eternal God who was before all things came into being.

The creation account in [ref:1 Mos 1:1-3|Genesis 1:1-3] shows that God created by His word ("God said, Let there be light"). John identifies this creative Word (Logos) as a person who was with God and was Himself God—the divine agent of all creation.

In [ref:Ordsp 8:22-30|Proverbs 8:22-30], Wisdom speaks of having been with God from the beginning, before anything was created. The parallel to the Logos who was "with God" (πρὸς τὸν θεόν) from eternity is clear, and Jewish wisdom tradition forms the background for John's theology of the Logos.

[ref:Sal 33:6|Psalm 33:6]: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made." Here God's word is directly linked to creative power, confirming John's identification of the Logos as the divine agent of creation.

[ref:Jes 55:11|Isaiah 55:11]: God's word goes out from Him and does not return empty, but accomplishes what He desires. This underscores the effective power and divine origin of the Word, in line with John's portrayal of the Logos as actively working in creation.

[ref:Jes 40:8|Isaiah 40:8]: "The word of our God stands forever." The eternal permanence of the Word points to John's presentation of the Logos as eternally existing—he "was" (ἦν, imperfect) in the beginning, without any beginning to His own existence.

[ref:Kol 1:15-17|Colossians 1:15-17] describes Christ as the image of the invisible God, born before all creation, and that all things were created through Him and for Him. This is a close parallel to John's statement that the Logos was with God and was God, and that all things were made through Him.

[ref:Heb 1:1-2|Hebrews 1:1-2]: God has spoken through His Son, whom He appointed heir of all things and by whom He made the universe. This confirms the Son's role as God's eternal Word and agent of creation, in agreement with John's prologue about the Logos.

[ref:1 Joh 1:1-2|1 John 1:1-2] speaks of "the Word of life" who was from the beginning and who was with the Father. The same author uses similar language and confirms the pre-existence of the Word and His fellowship with God the Father.

[ref:Åp 19:13|Revelation 19:13]: The heavenly rider bears the name "the Word of God" (ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ). This identifies the exalted Christ with the eternal Logos and confirms the divinity and eternal existence of the Word.

[ref:Fil 2:6|Philippians 2:6]: Christ was "in the form of God" and did not consider equality with God something to be grasped. This confirms the divinity of the Logos—"the Word was God" (θεὸς ἦν ὁ λόγος)—as a central part of early Christian confession.

[ref:Joh 17:5|John 17:5]: Jesus asks the Father to give Him the glory He had with the Father "before the world existed." This confirms the pre-existence of the Logos and His fellowship with the Father before creation, in agreement with the prologue.

[ref:Joh 1:14|John 1:14]: "And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us." This is the direct continuation of the hymn to the Logos and shows that the eternal Word who was God took on human nature—the incarnation.

[ref:Joh 1:18|John 1:18]: "No one has ever seen God. The only Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, He has made Him known." This elaborates that the Logos—the Son who is God—reveals the Father, and completes the statement that the Word was "with God" and "was God."

[ref:Joh 20:28|John 20:28]: Thomas confesses about Jesus: "My Lord and my God!" (ὁ κύριός μου καὶ ὁ θεός μου). This is the climactic confession of John's Gospel, confirming the declaration of the prologue: "the Word was God."
